title: Cap. 4 Mem. 3: Triple proof — mercy, Christ the Head, viator vs damned
pass_a_gloss: Possibility of having faith for any viator confirmed by three arguments. (1) From Divine mercy: Prosper — God takes from no one still on the way the path of correction, nor strips anyone of possibility of good; fixed law of remissio/life for any penitent/believer — Ezek 33:11 Nolo mortem impii. So not only absolute but ordinary power: any unbeliever/impious can be given true penitence & saving faith. Rom 11:23 God can re-graft Jews; Apoc 2:21 gave time to repent. Whole life-space given so conversion can be saving any moment (Ezek 18:21-22) — God reserved ability by ordained power to infuse faith/penitence grace to any not yet damned to hell. Put no one outside possible salvation-state whom God’s patience lets live. (2) From Christ the Head vs any viator: natural head influences only united members; mystical Head can act on separated members infusing vivifying grace for union. Aquinas 3.8.1: Christ head of all humans by degrees — principally those united by glory/actual grace; less principally those who by ordinary Divine law can still be united (whether potency reduced to act or not); of those with no potency to receive Christ’s influx he is in no way Head = only the damned (no redemption from hell by promulgated will). Faith-potency for anyone still in this life founded in Christ’s most sufficient Head-virtue + said mercy opening whole life to reception. (3) From different condition of viators vs those who reached term: theologians agree viator’s will flexible to good; damned will immoveably fixed in evil. After this life state of bad immobile (Damascene: what fall is to angels, death to humans; Eccles 11:3 tree falls where it lies). In this mortal life malice mutable → by ordinary power any unbeliever can be illuminated, impenitent converted, impious justified/saved. 2 Tim 2:25-26 instruct opposers — God may give repentance to know truth. 2 Pet 3:9 Lord patient, not willing any perish. Augustine Ep.54: no place for correcting morals but this life. Clement: no time too late/early to recover soul’s health while alive. Who will/won’t receive faith before exit = secret of will; but potency to faith/penitence remains to life’s end — would be vain unless reduced to act in some; that not in all → partly secret will, partly manifest human wickedness. From capacity not reduced to act in many → God manifests greater mercy to elect, clearer justice to impious unbelievers — so potency not vainly granted. Alvarez De auxiliis 105: potency not vain if reduced to some acts not every possible act (math capacity not vain though many lack teachers). Likewise faith/penitence potency present to all viators by fixed Divine law not vain though God does not make all believe/repent.
pass_b_english: That possibility of having faith, which looks to any wayfarer, is confirmed by a triple argument. First, one drawn from Divine mercy. For God, as Prosper speaks, takes from no one (still constituted on the way) the path of correction, nor strips anyone of the possibility of good. Moreover he has fixed a law concerning granting remission of sins and eternal life to any penitent and believing person: I do not will the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live ([[Ezekiel 33:11 >> Bible:Ezekiel 33:11]]). Therefore not only according to God’s absolute power, but according to ordinary power, any unbeliever and impious person can be gifted with true penitence and saving faith. Of the unbelieving Jews the Apostle truly says ([[Romans 11:23 >> Bible:Romans 11:23]]): God is able to graft them in again. And of all contumacious sinners it is rightly affirmed in God’s person ([[Revelation 2:21 >> Bible:Revelation 2:21]]): I gave them time that they might repent, and they were unwilling to repent. He who has so granted human beings the whole span of this life that in any moment of it conversion to God can be saving for them, according to that most celebrated saying of the Prophet ([[Ezekiel 18:21–22 >> Bible:Ezekiel 18:21]]), If the wicked shall have done penitence from all his sins, etc., I will not remember all his iniquities — the same has also reserved to himself that according to his ordained power he can infuse the grace of faith and penitence into anyone not yet damned to the underworld. Hence it is that we ought to put no one outside a possible state of salvation whom God’s patience allows to live.

Second, the same can be shown by an argument drawn from the respect of Christ the Head toward any of the wayfarers. For although a natural head does not have power of influencing except into members conjoined and united, yet this mystical Head can act upon separated members and pour into them vivifying grace by which they are united to him. In which sense Aquinas not inconveniently lays down (Part 3, question 8, article 1) that Christ is the head of all human beings, but according to diverse degrees. He is called Head principally of those who are united to him by glory, or by grace actually communicated; less principally of those who according to God’s ordinary law can still be united to him, whether that power is to be reduced into act or not: but of those who are in no potency to receive Christ’s influx he can in no way be called Head. Such, however, ought to be judged all and only the damned; because according to God’s promulgated will there is no redemption from the underworld. The power of having faith, then, as to anyone still constituted in this life, is founded in the most sufficient virtue of Christ the Head for influencing, and in the aforesaid mercy of God, who according to the common law willed the whole span of this life to lie open for receiving.

Last, that the condition of penitence and faith, under which Christ’s death is applicable to any human being unto salvation, is possible while we live here, is plain from the diverse condition of human beings while they are wayfarers and after they have come to the term. By the consent of all Theologians the will of any wayfarer is for this state flexible toward the good; just as, on the contrary, the will of the damned for that state is immoveably hardened in evil. However clear it is. That after this life the state of bad human beings is immobile and plainly immutable, no one doubts. For as Damascene rightly has it, book 2, chapter 4: What the fall is to angels, the same is death to human beings. If a tree shall have fallen, whether toward the south or toward the north, in whatever place it shall have fallen, there it will be ([[Ecclesiastes 11:3 >> Bible:Ecclesiastes 11:3]]). On the contrary, the will is flexible and the malice of human beings constituted in this mortal life is mutable, so far that by God’s ordinary power any unbeliever can be illuminated, any impenitent converted — in a word, any impious person justified and saved. Whence that of the Apostle ([[2 Timothy 2:25–26 >> Bible:2 Timothy 2:25]]): Those who are affected with a contrary mind are to be instructed with gentleness: if at some time God may give them that repenting they may acknowledge the truth and receive soundness of mind. He therefore hints that these things can still be done, and ought to be hoped for by us. Not unlike is that of Peter ([[2 Peter 3:9 >> Bible:2 Peter 3:9]]): The Lord is patient toward us, not willing that any perish, but that all tend to repentance. There is no other place for correcting morals than in this life, says Augustine, Letter 54. But in this life while we are, no time is either too late or too early for recovering the soul’s health, as Clement of Alexandria truly has it in the Stromata. Who is going to receive faith and penitence from God before he exits life, who is not going to receive, is a secret hanging from his will; but that the very power unto faith and penitence remains to the extreme period of this life — although such a power would indeed be in vain unless in some it were reduced to act; but that it is not reduced in all is to be referred partly to God’s secret will, partly to the manifest wickedness of human beings. Under both respects, from a capacity or power unto faith and salvation least reduced into act as to many, there follows for God a greater manifestation of his mercy toward the elect, a clearer manifestation of justice toward the impious unbelieving and impenitent: and therefore such a power is not granted them in vain. Alvarez well, On Helps, disputation 105: For some power not to be in vain, it is not required that it sometime be reduced to every act it can produce; but it suffices that it be reduced to some, or several. For just as no one would truly say that the power of perceiving the mathematical disciplines is given to human beings by nature in vain, although many capable of these disciplines do not find masters who actually instruct them in the same; so no one will have affirmed that this power of believing and repenting is present in vain to all wayfarers by God’s fixed law, although God does not effect in all that they believe, that they repent.
source_text:
Possibilitas illa habendi fidem, quae viatorem quemvis respicit, triplici argumento confirmatur. 1. Primo a misericordia Divina ducto. Deus enim, ut loquitur Prosper, nemini (in via adhuc constituto) correctionis adimit viam, nec quemquam boni possibilitate despoliat. Quinetiam legem fixit de indulgenda remissione peccatorum et vita aeterna cuivis poenitenti et credenti, Nolo mortem impii, sed ut convertatur impius a via sua, et vivat, Ezek. xxxiii. 11. Ergo non solum juxta potentiam Dei absolutam, sed secundum potentiam ordinariam quivis incredulus et impius potest vera poenitentia et fide salutifera donari. De Judaeis incredulis vere dicit Apostolus Rom. xi. 23, Potest Deus rursus eos inserere. Et de omnibus contumacibus peccatoribus in Dei persona recte affirmatur illud Apoc. ii. 21, Dedi illis tempus ut poenitentiam agerent, et noluerunt poenitere. Qui hominibus ita concessit totum hujus vitae spatium ut in quolibet ejusdem momento conversio ad Deum possit illis esse salutifera, juxta illud celeberrimum Prophetae dictum Ezek. xviii. 21, 22, Si impius egerit poenitentiam ab omnibus peccatis suis, etc. omnium iniquitatum ejus non recordabor; idem et sibi reservavit ut secundum ordinatam suam potentiam possit cuivis nondum ad inferos damnato gratiam fidei et poenitentiae infundere. Hinc est quod neminem ponere debemus extra possibilem salutis statum, quem patientia Dei sinit vivere.

2. Secundo, idem ostendi potest argumento ducto a respectu Christi Capitis, ad quemvis viatorum. Nam quamvis Caput naturale non habeat potentiam influendi nisi in membra conjuncta et unita, tamen hoc Caput mysticum potest agere in membra separata, et influere illis gratiam vivificam, qua mediante sibi uniantur. Quo sensu non incommode statuit Aquinas, Part. 3. qu. 8. art. 1, Christum esse caput omnium hominum, sed secundum diversos gradus. Principaliter dicitur Caput eorum qui sibi uniuntur per gloriam, aut per gratiam actualiter communicatam; minus principaliter eorum qui secundum legem Dei ordinariam possunt sibi adhuc uniri, sive ea potentia sit in actum reducenda, sive non: Illorum autem qui non sunt in potentia ad recipiendum influxum Christi nullatenus Caput dici potest. Tales autem judicari debent omnes et soli damnati; quia secundum promulgatam Dei voluntatem ab inferis nulla est redemtio. Potentia igitur habendi fidem, quoad quemvis in hac vita adhuc constitutum, fundatur in sufficientissima virtute Christi Capitis ad influendum, et praedicta Dei misericordia, qui secundum legem communem totum hujus vitae spatium patere voluit ad recipiendum.

3. Ultimo in loco, poenitentiae et fidei conditionem, sub qua mors Christi est cuivis homini ad salutem applicabilis, esse dum hic vivitur possibilem, patet ex diversa conditione hominum, dum viatores sunt, et postquam ad terminum pervenerunt. Ex consensu omnium Theologorum voluntas cujuscunque viatoris est pro hoc statu in bonum flexibilis; sicut e contra voluntas damnatorum pro illo statu in malo immobiliter obfirmata. Utcunque clarum est. Post hanc vitam immobilem et plane immutabilem esse statum hominum malorum, nemo dubitat. Nam ut recte Damascenus, lib. 2. cap. 4, Quod est angelis casus, idem hominibus mors. Si ceciderit lignum, sive ad austrum, sive ad aquilonem, in quocunque loco ceciderit, ibi erit, Eccles. xi. 3. E contra, flexibilis est voluntas et mutabilis malitia hominum in hac mortali vita constitutorum, adeo ut de potentia Dei ordinaria quivis incredulus possit illuminari, quivis impoenitens converti, uno verbo, quivis impius justificari et salvari. Unde illud Apostoli 2 Tim. ii. 25, 26, Cum lenitate erudiendos esse eos qui contrario animo sunt affecti: siquando det eis Deus ut resipiscentes agnoscant veritatem, ac mentis recipiant sanitatem. Innuit igitur haec posse adhuc fieri, et debere a nobis sperari. Non dissimile est illud Petri, 2 Petr. iii. 9, Patiens est Dominus erga nos, nolens ullos perire, sed omnes ad resipiscentiam tendere. Morum corrigendorum nullus alius quam in hac vita locus, inquit Augustinus, Epist. 54. In hac autem vita dum sumus, nullum tempus aut serum aut citum nimis ad recuperandam animae sanitatem, ut vere Clemens Alexandrinus Strom. lib. 2. Quis accepturus sit a Deo fidem et poenitentiam antequam exeat e vita, quis non accepturus, arcanum est pendens ex ejus voluntate; sed ipsam potentiam ad fidem et poenitentiam manere ad extremum usque hujus vitae periodum, etsi quidem frustra hujusmodi potentia esset nisi in aliquibus ad actum reduceretur: quod autem in omnibus non reducatur, partim ad arcanam Dei voluntatem, partim ad manifestam hominum pravitatem est referendum. Utroque respectu, ex capacitate sive potentia ad fidem et salutem, quoad multos in actum minime reducta, consequitur Deus majorem misericordiae suae manifestationem erga electos, justitiae manifestationem clariorem erga impios incredulos et impoenitentes: atque idcirco talis potentia non frustra illis conceditur. Bene Alvarez De auxiliis, disp. 105, Ut aliqua potentia non sit frustra, non requiritur ut aliquando sit reducenda ad quemlibet actum quem producere potest; sed sufficit quod reducatur ad aliquem, vel aliquos. Sicut enim nemo vere dixerit potentiam ad percipiendas disciplinas Mathematicas esse frustra datam hominibus a natura, quamvis multi capaces harum disciplinarum non inveniant magistros qui illos actu instituunt in eisdem; ita nemo affirmaverit hanc potentiam ad credendum et poenitendum frustra adesse omnibus viatoribus ex fixa Dei lege, quamvis Deus non efficiat in omnibus ut credant, ut poeniteant.
